title: QERA: an Analytical Framework for Quantization Error Reconstruction

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to establish the correct optimization objective for quantization error reconstruction, contrasting prior methods that minimize weight approximation error without theoretical justification. Paper [17] proposes Bias Compensation to minimize output error in quantization, which aligns with the purpose of addressing the relationship between quantization error and model output error. Paper [14] studies the effect of quantization on the loss landscape and its impact on accuracy, which indirectly relates to the purpose of optimizing quantization objectives. However, neither paper explicitly establishes the theoretical justification for minimizing layer output error as the correct optimization objective. Thus, no prior paper fully covers the purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves formal analysis contrasting minimizing weight approximation error (||W - W_tilde||_p) against minimizing layer output error (||y - y_tilde||_p), tracing the effect to the final model output error. Paper [14] analyzes the loss landscape structure under quantization, which involves studying the relationship between quantization and model loss but does not explicitly contrast weight approximation error with layer output error. Paper [17] minimizes output error through bias compensation but does not formally analyze the relationship between weight and layer output errors. No prior paper performs the specific formal analysis described in the contribution.

### Evaluation
The evaluation analytically demonstrates that minimizing weight approximation error does not guarantee reduced model output error, while minimizing layer output error is closely related to minimizing model output error. Paper [14] analyzes the loss landscape under quantization, which involves evaluating the impact of quantization on model loss, but does not use the same analytical design to contrast weight and layer output errors. Paper [17] evaluates bias compensation's effect on output error but does not analytically contrast weight and layer output errors. No prior paper uses the same evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is LLM quantization, efficient fine-tuning, and inference. Papers [1], [3], [9], [10], [11], [15], and [20] all address LLM quantization or efficient inference, making the domain covered.

### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to provide a theoretically grounded, closed-form way to compute the low-rank reconstruction terms \( A_k, B_k \), replacing hand-crafted heuristics like LQ-LoRA and LQER. This specific objective — replacing heuristic methods with a closed-form, theoretically grounded solution for low-rank reconstruction in the context of LLM quantization — is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While papers like [11] (LQER) and [1] (LRQ) address low-rank quantization and error reduction, they do not aim to replace heuristics with a closed-form analytical framework. Their focus is on empirical methods or heuristic-driven approaches, not on deriving a theoretical, closed-form solution.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves deriving QERA, an analytical framework with a closed-form solution to layer-output-error minimization, using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem for QERA-exact and a statistical assumption for QERA-approx. This mechanism is partially covered by prior work. Papers like [15] and [26] discuss the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem and its applications to low-rank approximations, providing the theoretical foundation for QERA-exact. Additionally, [12] and [13] address weighted low-rank approximation (WLRA), which overlaps with the statistical assumptions and approximations used in QERA-approx. However, no prior paper combines these elements into a unified framework specifically for layer-output-error minimization in LLM quantization.

### Evaluation
The evaluation facet involves Theorems 1-2, which provide exact and approximate solutions, and a computational efficiency analysis of QERA-approx. This evaluation design is covered by prior work. Papers like [15] and [26] provide theoretical proofs and closed-form solutions for low-rank approximations, which align with the evaluation design of proving theorems and analyzing computational efficiency. While the specific theorems and assumptions differ, the evaluation design itself — proving theoretical results and analyzing their computational implications — is not novel.

### Domain
The domain is LLM quantization, which is extensively covered by prior work. Papers like [1], [3], [4], [6], [7], and [11] all address LLM quantization, including post-training quantization (PTQ) and low-rank methods for reducing quantization error. While this contribution may target a specific sub-problem within LLM quantization, the general application area is well-established in the literature.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate that the analytical framework improves state-of-the-art QPEFT and PTQ methods under the same compute budget. Paper [4] (LQER) shares a substantively equivalent purpose, as it aims to recover model capability and reduce quantization errors in PTQ methods for LLMs, achieving nearly-lossless quantization. Similarly, paper [21] (Exploring Post-training Quantization in LLMs) conducts a comprehensive study of PTQ schemes and investigates methods to mitigate quantization errors, aligning with the goal of improving PTQ methods. Both papers address the same problem-class level objective of improving quantization methods for LLMs under resource constraints.

### Mechanism
The contribution applies QERA solutions to initialize/compute reconstruction terms in existing methods (LoftQ for QPEFT, ZeroQuant-V2 and LQER for PTQ). Paper [4] (LQER) uses low-rank approximation combined with quantization error reduction, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism of leveraging low-rank techniques to reconstruct quantization terms. Paper [8] (INT2.1) also employs low-rank adaptation to correct quantization errors, aligning with the mechanism of using low-rank methods for error reconstruction. Paper [18] (QDyLoRA) introduces dynamic low-rank adaptation for quantized models, which similarly involves low-rank decomposition and quantization error compensation. These papers share the same underlying primitive of using low-rank methods to address quantization errors.

### Evaluation
The contribution reports improvements in accuracy and perplexity metrics (Delta_acc and Delta_ppl) for quantized LLMs across benchmarks like GLUE, six LLM tasks, and WikiText2. Paper [4] (LQER) evaluates quantization performance using similar metrics (accuracy and task performance) on downstream tasks, including multitask language understanding. Paper [21] (Exploring Post-training Quantization in LLMs) uses a systematic evaluation of PTQ methods across various benchmarks and tasks, including weight-and-activation quantization. Both papers employ the same evaluation design — benchmarking quantized LLMs on task performance metrics — even if the specific benchmarks differ.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM quantization. Paper [4] (LQER), paper [21] (Exploring Post-training Quantization in LLMs), and paper [8] (INT2.1) all address LLM quantization, focusing on improving PTQ methods and reducing quantization errors. This domain is well-established in prior work, and the contribution does not introduce a new application area.
